messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] HELP!
messages.body_plain:
Hi -- if you didn't figure out the kexpmv error yet, the error you got is with the kexpmv package.

This was addressed in this post:
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/biogeobears/Matzke_R_binaries%7Csort:date/biogeobears/bBYxbeJ5jcM/0yT72TkmAgAJ

Which refers to:
https://github.com/nmatzke/Matzke_R_binaries

Which says:
================
Archiving CRAN binaries of R packages (because CRAN only archives source code, not binaries)

This repository simply archives the CRAN-generated binaries of R packages necessary/useful for BioGeoBEARS. Initially these are: cladoRcpp (see also GitHub cladoRcpp), rexpokit (see also GitHub rexpokit), and kexpmv.

It seems to be a regular issue that CRAN changes its choice of compilers for C++ and FORTRAN. Most recently, in October 2019, packages were tested against gfortran/gcc10 (which is still in beta). When this happens, legacy FORTRAN code can throw CRAN warnings, despite having passed all previous checks, and then CRAN can decide to archive a package. This means it will no longer be visible in the "package search" functions in R.app or RStudio.

For archived packages, CRAN does keep the source code available, but the compiled binaries for Windows and Mac OS X disappear. This can be very inconvenient, because:

Binaries install very quickly, installing from source can take minutes (if it succeeds at all).

Binaries do not require compilation of the source code on the user's computer.

Therefore, binaries do not require that the user install the compilers gfortran and gcc. Installing these compilers is a lengthy process which can take hours (see e.g. https://solarianprogrammer.com/2017/05/21/compiling-gcc-macos/ for the Mac instructions, regularly updated for each new version of OS X). (See also macports for gcc10.)

GitHub versions of the packages also require compilation-from-source. If you have a "pure R" package (like BioGeoBEARS), this is easy and fast, but if the source code contains C++ or FORTRAN, getting the right compilers and settings can be onerous for non-advanced users.

Getting non-technical users to install gcc and gfortran compilers is onerous at best, and impossible in a 4-hour workshop.

Method

After a CRAN package is accepted, the binaries are typically made available by CRAN within a few days. They are in this section of the package page (this section is for the CRAN cladoRcpp page):

Windows binaries: r-devel: cladoRcpp_0.15.1.zip, r-release: cladoRcpp_0.15.1.zip, r-oldrel: cladoRcpp_0.15.1.zip
OS X binaries: r-release: cladoRcpp_0.15.1.tgz, r-oldrel: cladoRcpp_0.15.1.tgz

All I have done in the "Matzke_R_binaries" repository is put up the saved versions of these binary files.

Instructions

First, navigate to the most recent version number of a package, and click "Download" to download from GitHub.

Second, install the downloaded package manually:

In R.app on Macs, you would click Packages & Data -> Package Installer -> Packages Repository ("Local Binary Package" option) -> click "Install..." -> navigate to the saved binary file.

>From the R command line, type something like this:

install.packages(pkgs="/GitHub/Matzke_R_binaries/cladoRcpp/cladoRcpp_0.15.1_MacRrelease.tgz", lib="/Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Resources/library/", repos=NULL, type="binary")

...or, if you have used setwd() to have the working directory set to where the binary was saved, and if you are happy with the default install location, this will probably work:

install.packages(pkgs="cladoRcpp_0.15.1_MacRrelease.tgz", repos=NULL, type="binary")
================

Cheers,
Nick

I just checked, it worked fine for me, I'm attaching my process in R.app on the Mac.

However, it's possible that some new version of Mac OS X and/or R for Mac has broken old binaries.  Given that other people have had trouble, I will work on making kexpmv optional, it's only rarely used anyway.

PS: OK, I just removed kexpmv from "Imports" in BioGeoBEARS on GitHub. I just re-installed with:

remove.packages("kexpmv")
remove.packages("BioGeoBEARS")

(close R, reopen R)

library(devtools)
devtools::install_github(repo="nmatzke/BioGeoBEARS")

...and it seems to work fine.

If dependencies give you real problems you can always try:

devtools::install_github(repo="nmatzke/BioGeoBEARS", dependencies=FALSE)

...as recorded here: https://github.com/nmatzke/BioGeoBEARS

Cheers,
Nick

messages.subject: AICc test between models.
messages.body_plain:
Hello Nick and everyone,

Happy New Year.

I have a question. I recently ran BioGeoBEARS on a dated phylogeny, ran the 6 models and compared their AICc values.

Interestingly enough, the best model and the second best models have close AICc values. But their range estimates are different for some nodes.

I kind of did the comparison between the best model (bayarealike+j) and the second best (divalike+j) the same way the tutorial shows how to do between, for example, diva and diva+j. I did change the degrees of freedom to 3 for both.

What I got as a p-value of 0 (zero). Assuming what I did above is correct, it means that both hypotheses of range estimates are plausible, right?

The main questions here are actually:
1- Can I compare the AICc values between diva and bay models?
2- If yes, what is the proper way to do it?

This is the testtable:

alt null LnLalt LnLnull DFalt DFnull DF Dstatistic pval test tail AIC1 AIC2 AICwt1 AICwt2 AICweight_ratio_model1 AICweight_ratio_model2
DEC+J DEC -114.2 -114.3 3 2 1 0.23 0.63 chi-squared one-tailed 234.4 232.6 0.29 0.71 0.41 2.43
DIVALIKE+J DIVALIKE -81.48 -100.6 3 2 1 38.29 6.1E-10 chi-squared one-tailed 169 205.2 1 1.3E-08 75800000 1.3E-08
BAYAREALIKE+J BAYAREALIKE -80.28 -119 3 2 1 77.46 1.4E-18 chi-squared one-tailed 166.6 242 1 4.1E-17 2.43E+016 4.1E-17

BAYAREALIKE+J DIVALIKE+J -80.28 -81.48 3 3 0 2.4 0

166.6 169 0.77 0.23 3.32 0.3

Cheers

JP

messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] AICc test between models.
messages.body_plain:
Hi, thanks for the question...

On Wed, Jan 15, 2020 at 8:16 AM JP F <arapa...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hello Nick and everyone,
>
> Happy New Year.
>
> I have a question. I recently ran BioGeoBEARS on a dated phylogeny, ran the 6 models and compared their AICc values.
>
> Interestingly enough, the best model and the second best models have close AICc values. But their range estimates are different for some nodes.
>
> I kind of did the comparison between the best model (bayarealike+j) and the second best (divalike+j) the same way the tutorial shows how to do between, for example, diva and diva+j. I did change the degrees of freedom to 3 for both.

So, the example script runs a few model comparisons.

1. Likelihood ratio test. This compares only 2 models, and one must be nested inside the other one, e.g. DIVALIKE is nested inside DIVALIKE+J.  The LRT provides a p-value.  This is the context where "null" and "alternative" models make sense.  If the null model is true, then the more complex model should only get a significant likelihood improvement 5% of the time (at the 5% cutoff).  The logic of this test relies on the fact that, when models are nested, you really have one model, e.g. when j=0, DIVALIKE+J is identical to DIVALIKE.

In the table you pasted, the columns from "LnLalt" to "tail" are about the LRT.

2. AIC. This can compare any number of models, but it provides AIC model weights, rather than p-values.  The model weights basically provide a measure of relative plausibility.  They can be interpreted rather like Bayesian posterior probabilities, BUT the Bayesian-posterior-probabilities interpretation assumes the true model is in the set of models, which is never the case in real life. The philosophy of AIC is against the idea of p-values, so AIC proponents don't promote cutoffs, they just say "all we have is relative measures of probability, these decline smoothly, we should just use the relative measures directly."

3. AICc. This works the same as AIC, but has a correction for small sample-size bias. Use AICc if you have <50 data (species), above that amount AIC and AICc are basically identical.

>
> What I got as a p-value of 0 (zero). Assuming what I did above is correct, it means that both hypotheses of range estimates are plausible, right?

It's not correct. BAYAREALIKE+J is not nested inside of DIVALIKE+J, so the LRT cannot be used, and you cannot get a p-value on the difference.  Also, since both models have 3 free parameters, the difference in the number of free parameters is 0, so the degrees of freedom is 0, which I think means the chi-squared distribution which gives the p-value is undefined, so the p=0 result you got is probably an NA or something.

>
> The main questions here are actually:
> 1- Can I compare the AICc values between diva and bay models?
> 2- If yes, what is the proper way to do it?

The example script produces a pairwise comparison table for 3 pairs of nested models, like the one you pasted in.

But is also produces AIC and AICc tables comparing all 6 models together. I would just use the AICc table.

If 2 models differ in their estimate of ancestral ranges, well, uncertainty is a fact of life!  Often people will publish the estimate of history under the single-best AICc model, but if 2 models are close, they could publish both, or publish one and then discuss the places where there is a difference with another plausible model, etc. Another choice is model-averaging the ancestral range estimates, but I wouldn't worry about that until you feel like you understand the basics of AIC etc.

MAKE SURE to CAREFULLY read:

Advice on statistical model comparison in BioGeoBEARS.
http://phylo.wikidot.com/advice-on-statistical-model-comparison-in-biogeobears

BioGeoBEARS mistakes to avoid.
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid

Cheers,
Nick

>
> alt null LnLalt LnLnull DFalt DFnull DF Dstatistic pval test tail AIC1 AIC2 AICwt1 AICwt2 AICweight_ratio_model1 AICweight_ratio_model2

> > I have a question. I recently ran BioGeoBEARS on a dated phylogeny, ran the 6 models and compared their AICc values.
> >
> > Interestingly enough, the best model and the second best models have close AICc values. But their range estimates are different for some nodes.
> >
> > I kind of did the comparison between the best model (bayarealike+j) and the second best (divalike+j) the same way the tutorial shows how to do between, for example, diva and diva+j. I did change the degrees of freedom to 3 for both.
>
> So, the example script runs a few model comparisons.
>
> 1. Likelihood ratio test. This compares only 2 models, and one must be nested inside the other one, e.g. DIVALIKE is nested inside DIVALIKE+J.  The LRT provides a p-value.  This is the context where "null" and "alternative" models make sense.  If the null model is true, then the more complex model should only get a significant likelihood improvement 5% of the time (at the 5% cutoff).  The logic of this test relies on the fact that, when models are nested, you really have one model, e.g. when j=0, DIVALIKE+J is identical to DIVALIKE.
>
> In the table you pasted, the columns from "LnLalt" to "tail" are about the LRT.
>
>
> 2. AIC. This can compare any number of models, but it provides AIC model weights, rather than p-values.  The model weights basically provide a measure of relative plausibility.  They can be interpreted rather like Bayesian posterior probabilities, BUT the Bayesian-posterior-probabilities interpretation assumes the true model is in the set of models, which is never the case in real life. The philosophy of AIC is against the idea of p-values, so AIC proponents don't promote cutoffs, they just say "all we have is relative measures of probability, these decline smoothly, we should just use the relative measures directly."
>
> 3. AICc. This works the same as AIC, but has a correction for small sample-size bias. Use AICc if you have <50 data (species), above that amount AIC and AICc are basically identical.
>
>
>
>
> >
> > What I got as a p-value of 0 (zero). Assuming what I did above is correct, it means that both hypotheses of range estimates are plausible, right?
>
> It's not correct. BAYAREALIKE+J is not nested inside of DIVALIKE+J, so the LRT cannot be used, and you cannot get a p-value on the difference.  Also, since both models have 3 free parameters, the difference in the number of free parameters is 0, so the degrees of freedom is 0, which I think means the chi-squared distribution which gives the p-value is undefined, so the p=0 result you got is probably an NA or something.
>
>
> >
> > The main questions here are actually:
> > 1- Can I compare the AICc values between diva and bay models?
> > 2- If yes, what is the proper way to do it?
>
> The example script produces a pairwise comparison table for 3 pairs of nested models, like the one you pasted in.
>
> But is also produces AIC and AICc tables comparing all 6 models together. I would just use the AICc table.
>
> If 2 models differ in their estimate of ancestral ranges, well, uncertainty is a fact of life!  Often people will publish the estimate of history under the single-best AICc model, but if 2 models are close, they could publish both, or publish one and then discuss the places where there is a difference with another plausible model, etc. Another choice is model-averaging the ancestral range estimates, but I wouldn't worry about that until you feel like you understand the basics of AIC etc.
>
> MAKE SURE to CAREFULLY read:
>
> Advice on statistical model comparison in BioGeoBEARS.
> http://phylo.wikidot.com/advice-on-statistical-model-comparison-in-biogeobears
>
> BioGeoBEARS mistakes to avoid.
> http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid
>
> Cheers,
> Nick

messages.subject: Time Stratified Analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hi Nick,

  I am running a time stratified analysis with dispersal not allowed into an area until more recently than 25 mya. The tree that I am using has a single extant species in this area, and, this species is separated from its closest relatives by a long branch, with the ancestor existing ~45 mya. Therefore, I expected that the ancestor will be reconstructed as inhabiting one region, with dispersal to the terminal region occurring at some point along the branch.

However, the results of the analysis suggest that the common ancestor is widespread across two regions, including the region that is prohibited 25 mya. I am assuming that I am setting up the time stratified analysis incorrectly, but I am not sure how to fix it. I am attaching my timeperiods and dispersal multipliers here and am hoping you could take a look at them.

The disallowed area before 25 mya is "W" in the file.

Thanks!

--Elyse

messages.subject: optimization issue with GenSA
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

So, today, I noticed an odd case that might also answer a recent question about parameters not updating between the initial value ("init") and the estimated values ("est").

Basically, for this dataset, under DEC the initial parameter values were (as is common default) d=0.01, e=0.01.

After the end of the optimization run under GenSA, the estimated parameter values were d=0.01, e=0.01, and the log-likelihood was -671.

Suspicious, I changed the optimizer from GenSA to optimx -- that is this line in the example script:

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$use_optimx = "GenSA"

...to...

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$use_optimx = TRUE

Re-running the optimization, the lnL came out as -425, and the ML parameters were d=0.0009, e=0.0041.

So, clearly GenSA totally missed the boat in this case.  Looking at the optimization run under GenSA, it would explore d=0 or e=0, but apparently not values between 0.01 and 0.0000...  Obviously this is a huge problem, if the ML parameter values are in this range.

I have never seen this behavior before, and GenSA hasn't been updated since early 2018, so I don't think it can be a change in GenSA.  It is possible that one of the dependencies of GenSA has changed, producing this weird behavior.

Anyway, if you notice this kind of thing going on, make this change:

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$use_optimx = "GenSA"
-->
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$use_optimx = TRUE

Cheers,
Nick
